summary: Defines S/MIME version 3.1, a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Digital signatures give authentication, integrity and proof of origin, encryption gives confidentiality, and compression can also be used. It was replaced by RFC 5751.

plainLanguage.summary: Secure email can be signed like a letter and sealed in a locked envelope. This document says how email programs do it. It was replaced by RFC 5751.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email with smime
subtitle: How to sign, encrypt and compress MIME data with S/MIME version 3.1, built on the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

tldr.problem: Ordinary MIME email and other MIME data can be read and altered in transit, and nothing proves who sent it.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME 3.1 wraps a MIME entity in a CMS object (SignedData, EnvelopedData or CompressedData) and carries it as application/pkcs7-mime, or signs it in the clear with multipart/signed. The RFC also sets which algorithms agents must support.
tldr.outcome: Signatures give authentication, integrity and proof of origin, and encryption gives confidentiality. RFC 3851 has been obsoleted by RFC 5751.

facts.label: Minimum RSA key size
facts.value: Must not be under 512 bits; 768 bits or more recommended

today: RFC 3851 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 5751, which is the current S/MIME message specification to read. It replaced RFC 2633.

sections.title: What S/MIME Provides
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) gives a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Digital signatures provide authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin. Encryption provides data confidentiality. Version 3.1 also allows compression, which only reduces size and gives no security.

It is not restricted to mail: it can be used with any transport that carries MIME data, such as HTTP, and by automated agents, for example to sign software-generated documents. The RFC separates requirements for sending agents and receiving agents, and its general advice is to be liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send. Version 3.1 agents SHOULD interoperate as far as possible with S/MIME versions 2 and 3.
sections.plainLanguage: S/MIME lets a message carry a signature (who wrote it), a lock (who can read it), or both. It works for email and for anything else that moves MIME data around.

sections.title: CMS Options and Required Algorithms
sections.content:
S/MIME uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and narrows its many options so that implementations interoperate. Of the CMS content types, only Data, SignedData, EnvelopedData and CompressedData are used. SignedData applies a signature, EnvelopedData applies encryption, and CompressedData applies compression.

  • Digest: agents MUST support SHA-1; receiving agents SHOULD support MD5 for old S/MIME v2 objects.
  • Signature: receiving agents MUST support id-dsa-with-sha1 and rsaEncryption; sending agents MUST support one of them.
  • Key encryption: rsaEncryption MUST be supported, and Diffie-Hellman (ephemeral-static) SHOULD be.
  • Content encryption: tripleDES (DES EDE3 CBC) MUST be supported. RC2/40 SHOULD be supported by receiving agents, and AES at 128, 192 and 256 bits SHOULD be supported.

Sending agents SHOULD include signed attributes such as signingTime, sMIMECapabilities and sMIMEEncryptionKeyPreference. The capabilities attribute lists, in order of preference, what the signer can handle, so that others know how to encrypt to them. The encryption key preference attribute names which of the signer's certificates should be used for encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: To make sure everyone's programs understand each other, the document picks a short list of locks and signing methods that every program must know. A signature can also carry a little note saying which locks its owner likes best.

sections.title: Preparing and Wrapping a MIME Entity
sections.content:
The data to protect is always a canonical MIME entity. It is prepared in three steps: follow local conventions, convert leaf parts to canonical form, and apply an appropriate transfer encoding. Text parts MUST have line endings canonicalized to CR LF and should name their character set. To protect headers such as Subject, To and From, a sender MAY wrap a full MIME message in message/rfc822 before securing it.

The secured entity is then given to CMS, and the resulting object is wrapped in MIME. application/pkcs7-mime carries EnvelopedData, SignedData and CompressedData. Its optional smime-type parameter tells a mail client what is inside without decoding the ASN.1:

  • enveloped-data: EnvelopedData, file extension .p7m
  • signed-data: SignedData, .p7m
  • certs-only: SignedData with no content, .p7c
  • compressed-data: CompressedData, .p7z

Implementations MUST use MIME types and MUST NOT rely on file extensions. A message is treated as S/MIME if it is application/pkcs7-mime, if it is multipart/signed with protocol application/pkcs7-signature, or if it is application/octet-stream with suffix p7m, p7s, p7c or p7z.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is first tidied into a standard shape. Then it goes into a special envelope that is labelled on the outside with what was done to it, such as signed or locked.

sections.title: Enveloping, Signing and Compressing
sections.content:
Enveloped-only messages are built by preparing the entity, producing EnvelopedData, wrapping it in a ContentInfo, and inserting it in application/pkcs7-mime. A copy of the content-encryption key SHOULD also be encrypted for the originator. Without a signature, there is no integrity protection: ciphertext can be replaced so that the meaning changes.

Signed-only messages have two formats, and receiving agents MUST handle both. The first is application/pkcs7-mime with SignedData. It cannot be read without S/MIME software, but it resists changes by well-meaning intermediaries, such as line wrapping. The second, preferred for sending, is the clear-signing multipart/signed format: the first part is the signed entity and the second part is a detached signature of type application/pkcs7-signature (extension .p7s). Its protocol parameter MUST be application/pkcs7-signature, and the micalg parameter names the digest, such as sha1. Anyone can view such a message, with or without S/MIME software.

A multipart/signed entity sent over 7-bit transports MUST be represented as 7-bit text, because a gateway that changed the encoding would invalidate the signature.

Compressed-only messages use CompressedData, and S/MIME versions before 3.1 will not recognize them. Signing, encrypting and compressing can be nested in any order, and receivers MUST handle arbitrary nesting within reasonable resource limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking a message is simple, but a lock alone does not prove who sent it. A signed message can be sent in the open with the signature stuck on the side, so even people without special software can still read the message.

sections.title: Certificates and Key Generation
sections.content:
A receiving agent MUST provide some way to obtain recipients' certificates, and agents SHOULD let users store and protect correspondents' certificates. The RFC does not say how certificates are validated; that is covered by a companion document, RFC 3850. A sender that signs MUST have a certificate so that others can verify the signature, but S/MIME 3.1 does not require a particular request mechanism.

All key pairs MUST be generated from a good source of non-deterministic random input, and the private key MUST be protected. For RSA, a user agent SHOULD generate keys of at least 768 bits and MUST NOT generate keys shorter than 512 bits. A receiving agent SHOULD verify signatures with keys of any size over 512 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: To check a signature or lock a message for someone, you need their public certificate, like an official ID card. The secret key that goes with it must be kept very safe and made in a truly unpredictable way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls 40-bit encryption weak. It offers little real security over plaintext, and is never recommended unless the only alternative is no cryptography. A human-controlled sending agent SHOULD let the sender weigh the risks of RC2/40 before sending, and a sender who decides weak encryption is unacceptable MUST NOT use it. Agents SHOULD tell users how strong a message's protection is.

A sender SHOULD NOT send a copy of a message with weaker cryptography than the original, because an attacker could decrypt the weak copy to learn what the strong one says. EnvelopedData without a surrounding or enclosed SignedData allows undetected modification of the ciphertext. The order of signing and encrypting also matters: with encrypt-then-sign, the recipient can see the encrypted block is unaltered but cannot tell how the signer relates to the plaintext. With sign-then-encrypt, an attacker could change unauthenticated parts of the encrypted message.

The RFC also points to RFC 3218 on the adaptive chosen ciphertext vulnerability in PKCS #1 version 1.5, and to RFC 2785 on small-subgroup attacks on Diffie-Hellman.
sections.plainLanguage: A very short lock is easy to pick, so it is hardly better than no lock. Never send a hard-to-open copy and an easy-to-open copy of the same secret, because opening the easy one reveals the secret.
